Okay, let me try to break this down for someone who might not be familiar with all these terms. So, there's this problem where you want to make a computer understand and answer complicated questions about a big database of facts, like Wikipedia or something similar. People have tried different ways to do this before, right? Some use big networks of neurons that learn from lots of examples, others use rules and templates that tell the computer exactly what steps to take. But these methods have their own problems.

This paper is about creating a better way that combines both approaches. They call it "Cipitr" and it's a type of neural programming system. Instead of just learning a single big network, they're teaching the system how to build programs step by step. Each step is like a small instruction that helps answer the bigger question.

Now, here's where it gets interesting. Normally, when you teach a system like this, you give it examples of what the right answer should look like and tell it what's right or wrong. That's called "supervision." But for really hard questions, that's not always possible because you need a lot of data and you can't check every single answer manually.

So, what did the researchers do instead? They used something called a "reinforcement learning" technique. Think of it like teaching a kid to ride a bike. You don't tell them every move they should make, instead you reward them when they do something right and encourage them to keep trying. Similarly, their system gets a reward when it comes up with something that gets it closer to answering a question correctly.

They also made some smart choices about what kind of instructions (or "operators") their program can use. There are a bunch of different operations you could use to process information, just like there are different math operations (addition, subtraction, etc.). But not all of them would make sense in every situation. Their system learns which ones are useful and which aren't, based on what works best at solving the problems it faces.

Another cool thing they did was create a way to check if their instructions are making sense before they even start using them. Like having a checklist of rules that say, "If you're going to add two numbers, make sure they are both numbers first." This helps avoid mistakes early on and saves time by not having to go through the whole process of solving a problem only to find out there was a mistake in how it was set up.

To test how well their new system worked compared to existing ones (which they call "baselines"), they looked at two different sets of problems: one that was more straightforward and another that required more complicated thinking. Surprisingly, even though they didn't have direct supervision (like being told exactly which steps were correct), their approach performed better than some other methods that did have more direct guidance.

What's really neat about this isn't just that it works well on these specific problems though. What's even more impressive is how adaptable it seems. If they wanted to apply this to different kinds of databases or different sorts of information they could potentially do that too without needing to completely retrain the entire system.
